name: BCAA

lead: BCAAs are three essential amino acids found in dietary protein and sold as stand-alone powders and capsules. Lifters use them to feel less sore and recover faster, which means more frequent training and more muscle over time.

Leucine switches on the mTOR pathway that starts muscle protein synthesis, and that mechanism is well described in lab work. Human studies suggest possible reductions in muscle-damage markers and soreness, while effects on performance are described as neutral or unclear, and trials on physique outcomes from BCAA supplements specifically are limited.

paras: People sip BCAA drinks or take capsules before, during or after lifting, often while training fasted or on a calorie deficit. They are commonly stacked with a protein powder or creatine, and users usually notice soreness differences within days rather than visible size.

Sold as a dietary supplement. Higher circulating BCAAs are associated with obesity and insulin resistance, and some studies have raised questions about links with ALS in athletes and about lifespan in mice; these relationships are not fully established.

social.title: BCAA's impact health and lifespan indirectly via amino acid balance

angle.text: Lifters use BCAA powders around training to cut soreness and speed recovery, so they can train more often and build a more muscular physique. Leucine's role in switching on muscle protein synthesis is well described; trials of stand-alone BCAAs for muscle gain are limited.

lead: Branched-chain amino acids (BCAAs) are the three essential amino acids with a branched side chain: leucine, isoleucine and valine. Humans cannot synthesise them and obtain them from dietary protein [1]. They are sold as stand-alone powders and capsules, mainly to people who lift weights, with claims about muscle growth, recovery and reduced soreness.

Leucine activates the mTOR signalling pathway involved in muscle protein synthesis, which is the main biological rationale for supplements; animal work shows leucine stimulates translation initiation in skeletal muscle [1][2]. Human evidence for BCAA supplements specifically is more limited than the mechanistic work, and Wikipedia describes much of the exercise evidence as coming from small studies, animal models or reviews [1].

Separately, research has found that circulating BCAA levels are higher in people with obesity and insulin resistance, and animal studies have raised questions about long-term BCAA supplementation [3][4]. In looksmaxxing and bodybuilding communities BCAAs are discussed as a muscle-building and recovery aid.
infobox: Powders, capsules, drinks; also in dietary protein
Maple syrup urine disease product authorised in EU 2025 [1]
US Institute of Medicine 2002 values: leucine 42, isoleucine 19, valine 24 mg/kg/day [1]

paras: As a supplement, BCAAs are taken by gym-goers and athletes for muscle gain, exercise recovery and reduced delayed-onset muscle soreness [1]. Medically, BCAA preparations have been studied in liver disease (cirrhosis, sarcopenia), critical illness and perioperative muscle loss [5][6]. A product for acute episodes of maple syrup urine disease, an inherited condition in which BCAAs accumulate, was authorised in the EU in July 2025 [1].

Leucine stimulates mTOR-dependent initiation of protein synthesis in skeletal muscle, shown in rat experiments [2]. Wikipedia notes that early rat studies found leucine alone produced nearly the same effect as a full BCAA mixture [1]. Reviews describe BCAAs as nutrient signals as well as protein building blocks, with effects on metabolism beyond muscle [3][4].
In 2002 the US Institute of Medicine set recommended intakes for the three amino acids; diets meeting the protein recommendation generally supply these amounts [1].

Human work on BCAAs spans several areas. A 2009 study found that obese people had a metabolite signature suggesting increased BCAA catabolism, correlated with insulin resistance, and rats fed BCAA-supplemented high-fat diets stayed as insulin resistant as high-fat controls despite lower weight gain [7]. A 2014 review reported that circulating BCAAs tend to be raised in people with obesity and are associated with worse metabolic health and future type 2 diabetes [8].

For exercise, Wikipedia reports that a meta-analysis suggested BCAAs may lower creatine kinase and reduce delayed-onset muscle soreness, while effects on fatigue may partly offset one another, giving a net performance effect described as relatively neutral [1]. In hepatic encephalopathy, BCAAs may ease symptoms but benefit for mortality, nutrition or quality of life has not been shown [1].

Registered trials include a 40-person study of BCAAs and muscle in healthy volunteers (completed) [9], a phase 3 trial in cirrhotic patients with sarcopenia [5], a trial in patients having gastric cancer surgery [10] and a phase 2 concussion trial [11]. These registrations do not themselves report outcomes.

Some studies have linked BCAA-containing supplements to amyotrophic lateral sclerosis among athletes, though Wikipedia says any link remains to be fully established; mouse studies showed neuronal hyperexcitability [1]. In mice, BCAA supplementation alone reduced lifespan and promoted obesity in one cited study, whereas BCAA restriction extended lifespan in flies and male mice [1]. Researchers describe the BCAA-insulin resistance relationship as an association whose causal direction is still being studied [3][8].
